porch.text: Okay, so — that's Uncle Ray and Miss Pat, and this porch is basically where I learned what cards even were. Don't let the lemonade fool you. Ray bids low on purpose and then books high just to watch you do the math out loud — and Pat? Pat remembers every bid you made three hands ago. And three years ago. They're not the fastest table on the route, and they're not trying to be. Play patient, count honest, and don't try to out-talk them. Nobody out-talks this porch. We just gotta out-book 'em.

barbershop.text: Mr. Coleman and Miss June. Fifty years in that shop, and everything in it is by the book — including the game. No jokers here, Ace Down, so the deck is honest and so are they. Coleman's a retired teacher: he plays textbook, every book accounted for, no gifts. June's the one to watch, though. Quiet, exact — she bids what the mirrors show her, and she does not guess. Beating them ain't about tricks. It's about doing the plain thing right, every single hand, till they respect it.

rec-center.text: Lil' Man and Trey. Yeah, those two. Lil' Man beat me one summer and I stopped coming around — that's the history, so let's just put it on the table. Here's the real scouting report: they're loud because loud works. Twenty seconds a move, all that yelling, and pretty soon you're playing fast just to keep up — and fast is where the mistakes live. Lil' Man bids like momentum is a card, and some games he's a world-beater and some games he just... isn't. Trey's the echo — whatever Lil' Man says, louder. Play your speed, not theirs. Breathe between tricks.

cookout.text: Keisha and Teisha — the Twins. And before you ask: yes, it's as weird as it looks. They finish each other's sentences, each other's bids, everything. Keisha bids for two people like she's holding one big hand, because far as she's concerned, she is. Teisha's quieter, meaner — she plays her sister's cards as careful as her own. This is the first table on the route that actually counts what you throw away, so nothing's free anymore. The test here ain't them, it's us: do we cover each other like they do? That's Mama's standard, and they grade on it.

corner.text: Okay. Listen to me on this one. That's Smoke, and that's Redd, and this corner is the first table where the game can hurt you. My daddy owed these people. That bill is part of why we're here. Smoke counts everything — every card, every bag, every look — and he bids like the count is the whole conversation. Redd barely talks, and when he bids, he bids mean. They hunt nils for sport. Ours and theirs. So: no lazy bids, no free books, and if one of us goes nil, the other one guards it like rent money. Quiet table. Loud consequences.

church-basement.text: Mind your manners at this one — and your arithmetic. That's Deacon Ford, sweet as pie until the cards come out, and Sister Mae, who runs this basement like it owes her money. Mae ran this whole route herself, years back. Stopped one stop short. She doesn't talk about why, so I won't either. What I will say: nils are worth double down here, and these two treat a nil like a calling — planned, prayed over, and covered like family. Deacon preaches patience and practices it. Mae covers her partner the way she'd cover her own child. Play clean, guard your partner, and do not — do not — get caught grandstanding in Sister Mae's basement.

rooftop.text: Poet and Seven. I won't pretend I understand this table — nobody does, that's kind of the point of it. Poet talks like the game already happened and he's just telling you how. Riddles, prophecies, all that. Except his calls keep coming true, so laugh careful. Seven's said maybe ten words since 2019 — but his game is the blind nil. Up here it's always on and worth three hundred, and he calls it without looking, like scripture. These two play the deepest game on the route so far. Everything they throw means something. Watch what they keep, not what they say. Well — except Poet. Watch what he says too.

high-rise.text: Velvet and the Accountant. Start with what everybody gets wrong: Velvet smiles like she's lost and bids like she's broke. Neither one is true. She left our street with forty dollars and came back owning the view — she under-bids on purpose and then plays over her number, so don't you dare relax on her little bid. The Accountant is the opposite problem: no smile, no mercy, just math. He counts every card played and every bag owed, and his nil math has ended more runs than any pair alive. Nothing at this table is an accident. So we don't give them accidents.

the-pjs.text: Captain Block and Brick — the Captains. This is their street, their light, their table, and they play like the fence is a rule: nothing gets through. The Captain fell one stop short of the King in his own run, years ago, and instead of quitting he took the door — he's been pricing everybody who walks through it for twenty years. Brick doesn't talk, doesn't blink, doesn't react. Twice in twenty years, supposedly. Don't play to her — you can't read a wall. Play to the Captain's pride. This is home turf at full strength. We earn this one or we don't take it.

legends.text: Queenie and Ace. Take a second, because this is the history part. Queenie ran this route before it was a route — beat Vegas in '87 and stayed gracious about it for fifty years, which tells you everything about the kind of dangerous she is. Grace at full strength. Ace is her mirror: precise to the card, remembers every hand he's ever dealt — including the night the lights went out in '03, at the King's table. And Ace gambles. He'll nil at you smiling, because betting on people is the only bet he still enjoys. They're not guarding this table. They're guarding us from what's behind it.

king.text: The King of the Block — and the Ringer. Twenty-two years, nobody's taken this table. Not because he's magic. Because there's no mistake to wait for. The King counts everything, forgets nothing, and plays the cards in front of him instead of the name across from him — you should be so lucky as to get underestimated; you won't be. The Ringer? Nobody knows his name, nobody knows his game, and that blank page is the point — you can't scout what isn't written down. And the terms, so you hear them from me first: we have to beat them twice in a row. First win banks nothing. So pace yourself — this is two games wearing one crown.
